quote: Die kürzeste Entfernung 2er nicht sich schneidender {+und nicht+} [-?-] parallelen Graden finden d.h. gemeinsame Senkrechte
english: Find the shortest distance between two lines that neither intersect nor are parallel, i.e. their common perpendicular.
topic: A crossed-out geometric sketch about lines that neither intersect nor are parallel, using a chain of equal angles and segments, followed by a note on functional equations relating Dirichlet's principle, spherical functions, and electric charge distributions on spheres or circles.

triage.modern_statement: Given two straight lines that do not meet and are not parallel, construct the segment perpendicular to both (the common perpendicular) and show that it gives the shortest distance between them. In Euclidean 3-space these are skew lines. If the lines lie in one plane, as the crossed-out sketch may suggest, they must be ultraparallel lines in the hyperbolic (Bolyai-Lobachevsky) plane. In both settings the common perpendicular exists, is unique, and its length is the minimal distance.
triage.answered_by: This is a classical textbook result, not an open problem. For Euclidean skew lines the common perpendicular is standard solid and descriptive geometry. For the hyperbolic plane, Hilbert himself proved from his axioms that any two ultraparallel lines have a common perpendicular. The arXiv source cites this as Hilbert, ref. [10], p. 149; it is presumably his axiomatic treatment of Bolyai-Lobachevsky geometry, but I did not confirm the exact publication. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: Skew lines are lines in 3D that neither meet nor are parallel. The distance between them is the length of their common perpendicular, which is the shortest distance.
Descriptive geometry includes standard methods for locating the shortest connector (common perpendicular) of two skew lines in general position.
In hyperbolic geometry, lines that neither intersect nor are limiting parallel are called ultraparallel. The ultraparallel theorem says every such pair has a unique common perpendicular.
Hilbert proved from his axiom system for H^2 that any two ultra-parallel geodesic lines have a common perpendicular (cited as Hilbert, [10], p. 149).
Explicit constructions of the common perpendicular of two lines in 3-dimensional hyperbolic space are given in the literature.

triage.why: The note asks for a standard elementary construction, the common perpendicular, which already had well-known solutions. The 'chain of equal angles and segments' in the crossed-out sketch is in line with the hyperbolic-plane reading, which matches Hilbert's own work on Bolyai-Lobachevsky geometry, but the page alone does not settle whether he meant the Euclidean or the hyperbolic case. Either way it is a solved, textbook-level problem or a teaching exercise, not an open research question. Only later generalizations, such as to subspaces of H^n, appear in current papers.
